entries.why: `proRataListPrice` is a promotion allocation method — splitting a bundle's discount across components by list price. `prorate` on a subscription change is time-based against a plan. **Neither prices the unused remainder of an entitlement a guest already holds**, which is what a day-ticket-to-annual-pass upgrade needs, and the answer differs by entitlement kind: a multi-day ticket prorates on entries used, a membership on days elapsed.
entries.fix: Compute upgrade value from the entitlement's remaining worth, per entitlement kind.
entries.blockedNote: Ready. 2.14.12 confirmed pro-rated upgrade is required and unmodelled.
entries.closedBy: quoteUpgrade. proRataListPrice splits a bundle discount and prorate is time-based against a plan — **neither computes moving a ticket from one product to another.** The unused portion is the credit and what counts as unused depends on the entitlement. **The basis is returned with the quote**, because a guest disputing an upgrade price is disputing the basis.

entries.what: Person type is not modelled, so it cannot be changed on an upgrade.
entries.why: Adult, child, senior and resident exist as `ProductVariant.axisValues` — a variant axis, not an attribute of the ticket holder. Changing a child ticket to an adult one is therefore an exchange to a different product rather than an amendment, which works commercially and loses the fact that the same person aged. **It also blocks 2.9.17**: pricing by residency needs person type to be a property of the holder, not of the SKU.
entries.fix: Decide whether person type is a holder attribute alongside the variant axis.
entries.blockedNote: Ready. 2.13 walked without person type appearing as a holder attribute.
entries.closedBy: EntitlementTemplate.personType. Adult and child existed only as variant axis values, so an upgrade was a cancel-and-rebuy. **Recorded on the entitlement because the guest ages and the product does not.**

entries.what: An assisted transaction is not bound to a case.
entries.why: `startKioskAssist` records a staff member helping a guest and `createCase` records a service interaction; neither references the other, so the traceability 2.13.20 asks for has no link to follow. Both are in the same contract and `Case` already carries `relatedOrderId` as the precedent.
entries.fix: Reference the case on the assist session, following the relatedOrderId precedent.
entries.closedBy: Conversation.assistSessionId. startKioskAssist and createCase neither referenced the other, **so the traceability 2.13.20 asks for had no link to follow.** On the conversation because a case may span several assists and an assist belongs to at most one case.

entries.what: Media stock is not modelled — neither which stock a printer is loaded with, nor how much of it is left.
entries.why: `wristbandEncoder` is a device kind and `mediaKind` includes wristband, so encoding is covered and **the physical substrate is not**. A printer loaded with bronze, silver and gold ribbon cannot be told which to use, and 2.16.16 asks for stock levels of cards, wristbands and ticket rolls across locations. `RegisteredDevice.status` reaches `consumableLow` — a flag, not a count. The state model already says why it matters: *a wristband printer that runs out at 10am on a Saturday closes a gate.*
entries.fix: Model media stock as inventory, and name the loaded stock on the device.
entries.closedBy: ConfigureWorkstationRequest loadedMediaStockId and mediaStockRemaining. **A till that runs out of wristbands mid-queue is an outage nobody predicted.** Read-only, because the count comes from what was printed rather than from somebody estimate.

entries.what: No identity verification. A presented document is never checked against the entitlement holder.
entries.why: `idReader` and `biometricReader` are device kinds; `enrolFacePass` binds a face to an entitlement, which is enrolment rather than verification. 2.13.41 wants a document read and matched at the point of sale or gate, and 2.14.7 wants an annual-pass quota keyed to biometric identity. **CF-35 is open on biometric data under PDPL** — heightened protection, explicit consent, DPIA — so the design question and the legal one arrive together.
entries.fix: Model verification distinctly from enrolment, with the PDPL position settled first.

entries.what: No incident or exception log at the till.
entries.why: `recordNoSale` is the only till event captured for its own sake. A voided sale, a failed print, a refused card, a disputed refund — the things a supervisor reviews at close — have nowhere to be recorded with a reason. `shift` already carries variance and its approval, which is the same shape.
entries.fix: An exception log on the shift, with a reason code.
entries.blockedNote: Ready. 5.9 walked — shift variance is computed and no till exception log exists.
entries.closedBy: Shift.incidents — no-sale, drawer open, override, void after payment, dispute. **The log a cash-up investigation starts from**, and a shift that balances with four unexplained no-sales is not a shift that balanced.

entries.what: No performance targets anywhere in the package.
entries.why: 2.14.3 asks for sub-second transactions and 2.14.4 for fast POS start. **Performance targets are one of the three artefact classes still open** — `closed_classes.json` lists twelve of fifteen and this is one of the three that is not. A latency budget stated late is a latency budget met by accident.
entries.fix: State latency budgets for the operations on the critical sale path.
entries.closedBy: PerformanceTarget on the six critical-path operations. **A budget on every operation is a budget nobody measures.** validateAccess at 200ms because a turnstile has a guest walking at it, createPayment at 1500ms because the gateway is most of it. **Measured at the edge**: a 200ms service behind a 900ms gateway is a 900ms turnstile to the guest.

entries.what: No benign membership freeze.
entries.why: `suspendEntitlement` exists and is a **sanction** — its own description reads *fraud, a chargeback, a behavioural ban*, denying at the gate with a stated reason so an operator knows what to say. A guest pausing an annual pass for three months abroad is the opposite act and should extend validity by the frozen period rather than deny entry. Using one operation for both would put a fraud reason on a courtesy.
entries.fix: A freeze that suspends consumption and extends validity, distinct from suspension.
entries.closedBy: `freezeEntitlement` added — consumption stops and validity extends. **Distinct from `suspendEntitlement`, which is a sanction and does not extend.**

entries.what: No recurring guest billing — cycles, auto-renewal on a stored payment method, retry schedules, grace periods, dunning, downgrade or billing statements.
entries.why: **`subscription` looks like the answer and is not.** It is the Control Plane, running outside any cell because it provisions cells, and it bills tenants for the platform. A guest paying monthly for an annual pass is a different ledger, a different payer and a different failure mode. **The `subscription` state model already mentions a dunning period and no contract declares one** — the capability search flagged it as present only in states, which is CF-49's shape. Recurring guest billing also brings stored card credentials, mandates and PCI scope that the current payment model does not carry.

entries.what: No digital waiver anywhere — no document, no version, no acceptance, no signature, no linkage to ticket issuance.
entries.why: `signature` appears only on maintenance work-order attachments and inspection items; `signaturePad` is a device kind with nothing to sign. **Fourteen requirements and none of them partly served.** Three make it more than a form: **2.15.9 makes ticket issuance conditional on acceptance**, which puts a waiver in the purchase path rather than beside it; **2.15.13 requires the exact accepted version retained**, which is legal evidence and the same reasoning `white-label.Policy` already applies — *a guest who consented to version 3 consented to version 3*; and **2.15.7 requires parental consent for a minor**, which is a distinct legal act with its own capture and retention. A waiver is what a venue relies on after an injury, so an unversioned or unretrievable one is worse than none.
entries.closedBy: FormDefinition with requiresSignature, versioning and guardian consent. **2.15.13 requires the exact accepted version retained** — a submission pointing at a form that has since changed proves nothing. **A minor cannot waive their own rights**, so onBehalfOfSubjectId names the guardian.

entries.what: No ticket template, no proof print, and no automatic media-type selection.
entries.why: A venue changing its ticket artwork has no path that is not a code change, and 2.16.6 asks to print a proof without processing a sale — the equivalent of `white-label.createPreview`, which exists for storefront configuration and not for media. Template versioning would join the BL-058 cluster.
entries.fix: A media template with fixed and dynamic fields, previewable, following the white-label preview precedent.
entries.closedBy: TicketTemplate and printTicketProof. **Artwork is checked by looking at it, and the only way to look at it was to sell something.** selectionPriority answers automatic media-type selection — a kiosk with no printer and a guest with no smartphone need different answers. **A proof is marked as one, because a proof that can be mistaken for a ticket is a ticket.**

entries.what: Media cannot be recycled, and replacement does not automatically disable the previous medium.
entries.why: A wristband or plastic card released from one guest and reassigned to another is routine at a water park and has no operation. Replacement is the sharper half: **F23 already states the rule for contractor badges — reissued, and the old one blacklisted, both must happen** — and that rule is not stated for guest media, so a replaced wristband may still open a gate.
entries.fix: Release and reassign, and blacklist-on-replace following the F23 rule.
entries.blockedNote: Ready, and 3.2 enlarged it. Media swap (3.2.4) joins recycling and replacement, and F23's rule — reissued, and the old one blacklisted, both must happen — is stated for badges and not for guest media. `access.addBlacklistEntry` is the mechanism that would enforce it.
entries.closedBy: TicketTemplate.isRecyclable and recycleAfterDays. **An RFID wristband handed back at the exit is stock, not waste**, and nothing released it — so a reissued card served two entitlements. **Replacement disables the previous medium automatically** (the F23 rule), because relying on somebody remembering to blacklist it is how they walk in on the old one.

entries.what: No fraud detection over scan behaviour — device sharing, simultaneous sessions, excessive activations, face-change audit.
entries.why: **The data is complete.** `ScanEvent` records access point, ticket, media, outcome, deny reason, direction, operator, device and override with reason, so every input a detector needs is captured. What is absent is the detection, and CF-73 parked the fraud engine as needing a season of history. **Some of this needs no model at all** — one media code presented at two gates at once is a rule, not a prediction — and that half is worth separating from the parked engine. **Unblocked 18 August** — it was held on CF-73, which closed. A blocker that outlives its conflict is the backlog decaying in the way this apparatus exists to prevent.
entries.fix: Split rule-based scan anomalies from the parked model-based engine.
entries.closedBy: AccessPoint.scanAnomalyRules. **Rule-based and deterministic, separated from the parked model-based engine** — two entries eight seconds apart at gates four hundred metres apart is arithmetic, not a model.

entries.what: Biometric checking cannot be switched on or off per ticket type.
entries.why: `FacePassEnrolment` binds a face to a subject and entitlement. The requirement wants the *requirement* for a biometric check to be a property of the product — memberships checked, day tickets not — which belongs on the entitlement template or the admission profile, neither of which carries it. **CF-35 is open on biometric data under PDPL**, and a per-product switch is how a venue limits the population it enrols.
entries.fix: A biometric-required flag on the admission profile.

entries.what: Face Tag — temporary facial storage discarded when the ticket expires — is not distinguished from Face Pass.
entries.why: `FacePassEnrolment` carries `expiresAt` and `isActive`, so a lifetime exists. **The retention obligation is what differs**: an enduring enrolment with explicit consent is one legal posture, a same-day tag deleted at close is another, and under PDPL the second is far easier to justify. Storing both as one record with a date makes the stricter rule depend on a field nobody enforces.
entries.fix: Model tag and enrolment as distinct kinds with distinct retention.

entries.what: Emergency drop-arm mode is not distinguished from a closed turnstile.
entries.why: `TurnstileMode` has `closed`, which stops entry. The requirement wants an emergency mode where the arm drops, nobody scans and **nothing is counted** — and an emergency is precisely when the in-park figure matters most, because it is the number the fire officer asks for. Recording an evacuation as a closure would leave the count frozen with people leaving.
entries.fix: Add an emergency mode to TurnstileMode, stated to suspend counting, and record its activation.
entries.closedBy: AccessPoint.operatingMode. **A closed turnstile and one in emergency drop-arm mode look the same in the model and are opposite in meaning** — closed refuses everybody, drop-arm lets everybody through, and it exists for an evacuation. **freeFlow counts without validating and must be visibly distinct from a broken reader.**

entries.what: No hotel room-card integration at access points.
entries.why: A room card read at a venue gate has no media source and no entitlement behind it. `MediaKind` includes `magstripe`, so the read is covered and the entitlement is not. Belongs with the integration sweep — a hotel PMS is another named third party absent from the register. **Unblocked 18 August** — held on CF-128, now closed. **A blocker that outlives its conflict is the backlog decaying in the way this apparatus exists to prevent**, and this is the second time in one day it happened.
entries.fix: Model a room card as an externally-issued entitlement source.
entries.closedBy: AccessPoint.externalCredentialSources. **A hotel room card admitting a guest — externally issued, validated without having been sold.** The entitlement is created on first use, because a hotel with 400 rooms does not want 400 entitlements a night for guests who never visit.

entries.what: No podium feature — a supervised validation position directing groups, with its own device behaviour and reporting.
entries.why: The requirement describes a staffed position rather than a gate: validating several parties, directing them, and reporting separately from turnstiles. An `AccessPoint` with a handheld covers the scan and not the supervision model or the distinct reporting.
entries.fix: Confirm with the client what a podium does that a staffed access point does not.
entries.closedBy: AccessPoint.operatingMode podium — **a supervised validation position where staff direct a group through, validating by eye against a list.** It scans nothing, and it is how school parties actually enter.

entries.what: Attribute-based access control does not exist — forty-eight requirements against a role-based model chosen deliberately.
entries.why: `Grant` is principal, role, permission, scopePath, effect and a validity window. **That is role-based with scope inheritance, and it is a decision rather than an omission** — ADR-0002 makes authorisation user-driven rather than workstation-driven, ADR-0018 resolves up the scope tree nearest-ancestor-wins, and `resolvePermissions` and `Session.permissionsByScope` implement it. 3.3 asks for policies evaluated against membership, accreditation, customer segment, venue, attraction, device, capacity, occupancy and risk attributes, with a visual builder, reusable templates, versioning, pre-deployment simulation and an approval workflow. **That is a policy engine, and roughly a third of the requirements are already met by the existing model** — real-time evaluation, caching, offline evaluation, least privilege, temporary grants with automatic expiry, audit, tenant and venue scoping, inheritance. **The decision is whether the remaining two thirds justify replacing a settled architecture**, and it is worth noting that 3.3 mixes staff authorisation with guest admission rules, which the package deliberately separates into `identity` and `access`.

entries.what: Payment at exit for parking contradicts a decision already recorded.
entries.why: `access.yaml` states that pay-per-hour parking unrelated to a ticket runs on the parking system's own POS, decided 14 August. 3.4.1 asks for payment upfront **or at exit**. Either the decision needs restating to cover the exit case or the requirement is out of scope, and the contract's own text is the evidence either way. Second appearance after 19.2.78. **Unblocked 18 August** — held on CF-69, now closed.
entries.fix: Reconcile with the 14 August parking scope decision.
entries.blockedNote: Ready. 7.4.30 restated per-hour parking rates, which the 14 August scope decision excludes.
entries.closedBy: Declined by CF-124 (Qossai, 14 August) and recorded 18 August. **Pay-per-hour parking runs on the parking system own POS** — taking money at exit would make the venue an acquirer for parking, with a settlement path and tax treatment nobody designed. Parked with a decision behind it rather than left as a gap.

entries.what: Per-component redemption rules inside a bundle are not stated.
entries.why: Components keep their own entitlement template and envelope, so inventory, capacity and validity are independent by construction — the structure is right. What is unstated is whether redeeming one component affects the others, and whether a partly-redeemed bundle can be refunded.
entries.fix: State component independence on redemption and refund.
entries.blockedNote: Ready. 4.1 walked and component redemption rules did not appear; 4.4.20 restated it for retail kits.
entries.closedBy: PromotionConditions.componentRedemption — allTogether, independently or sequenced. **A park-plus-lunch bundle where lunch may be used another day behaves differently from one where both must be used on the same visit, and the difference is revenue recognition rather than convenience.**

entries.what: No payment-type or card-issuer promotion condition.
entries.why: `PromotionConditions` carries fifteen fields — variants, kinds, categories, quantity, basket value, channels, days, times, membership tiers, coupon, first purchase, performances, advance days — **and none of them is tender or issuer**. Bank-funded promotions are ubiquitous in the region, and they are not only a discount rule: the issuer normally reimburses, so the promotion needs settlement attribution as well as a condition. **Evaluation order also breaks** — a discount conditioned on tender cannot resolve before the tender is chosen, and promotions currently evaluate on the cart.
entries.fix: A tender and issuer condition, with a settlement attribution, and a stated evaluation point.
entries.closedBy: PromotionConditions.paymentMethod and issuerBins. **10% with a Network International card is a real campaign a bank co-funds** and it was unexpressible. **Evaluated at payment rather than at cart**, which is the awkward part: the basket total must be allowed to move after the tender is chosen.

entries.what: No promotion simulation before launch, and no A/B testing of variants.
entries.why: **The package simulates in four places** — `dryRun` on performance cancellation, revenue recognition, FX revaluation and period close, each an expensive irreversible act. A promotion is the same category: `budgetCap` stops it after the money is spent, and nothing estimates exposure beforehand. `analysePromotionConflicts` is the nearest thing and answers a different question.
entries.fix: A dry-run estimate on promotion creation, following the existing dryRun pattern.
entries.closedBy: simulatePromotion and setPromotionVariants. **A promotion is priced by guessing until it runs** — run it against a past period and the answer is arithmetic. **incrementalOrders is the number nobody computes and the one that decides whether a campaign made money.** A/B split is by stable hash of the subject, because **a guest who sees 10% on Monday and 15% on Tuesday has learned to wait.**

entries.what: Which tenders a sales channel accepts is not configurable.
entries.why: `Payment.tender` records what was used. Nothing constrains what may be offered — a kiosk that should not take cash, or a web channel that should not offer wallet, has no way to say so. Pairs with BL-004 tenant payment-provider configuration.
entries.fix: Payment-method availability by channel and venue.
entries.closedBy: PaymentProvider.acceptedOnChannels. **A kiosk taking cash and a website taking cards is not a policy either could infer.**

entries.what: No payment gateway abstraction, no routing, and no card tokenisation.
entries.why: `Payment` carries `providerName` and `providerReference`, which **records** a provider and does not abstract one. `paymentGateway`, `gatewayRouting`, `tokenization` and `cardOnFile` return nothing anywhere. **Three things depend on tokenisation and none of them can be built without it**: recurring membership billing (CF-129), wallet auto-reload, and one-click guest checkout. Routing by country, currency, card type or cost is a commercial lever a multi-region operator expects, and it interacts with ADR-0014 cell-per-region. **Tokenisation also moves the PCI boundary**, which is a compliance decision rather than a design one. **Lane changed to deferred 18 August** — the decision behind it was taken (CF-134, CF-131, CF-125) and what remains is build, not a conversation.
entries.closedBy: PaymentProvider, PaymentRouting and PaymentToken. **Payment carried providerName, which records a provider and does not abstract one** — and CF-131 confirmed two gateways, which is the number that forces this: one can be hard-coded and two cannot. **Tokenisation is the keystone**: recurring billing, auto-reload, one-click and payment links all waited on it. The card never reaches the platform, and storing one needs its own consent purpose because **a token taken without it is a card kept on a guest behalf they never agreed to**.

entries.what: Reconciliation is per provider rather than across every money source.
entries.why: `ingestSettlementFile`, `getSettlement`, `listSettlementExceptions` and `resolveSettlementException` are good and provider-scoped. 4.2.19 wants POS, online, gateway, bank, wallet and loyalty reconciled as one view — which is what a finance team actually does at close, and what `getTrialBalance` half serves.
entries.fix: One reconciliation view across sources.
entries.blockedNote: Ready. 5.7.90 restated it — reconciliation is per provider, not across bank, gateway, POS and wallet.
entries.closedBy: getUnifiedReconciliation across POS, gateway, bank, wallet and ledger. **A discrepancy is usually the gap between two sources rather than inside one**, so the variance is the answer — a view showing four sources each balanced against itself has not reconciled anything.

entries.what: No payment fraud rules and no chargeback or dispute management.
entries.why: **Largely rule-based and distinct from the parked engine.** Velocity checks and duplicate-card detection need no history; a card used five times in ten minutes is a rule. Chargebacks are the sharper omission — `finance.disputeObligation` exists for inter-entity obligations and there is nothing for a card dispute, which has deadlines, evidence bundles and money moving back out. Missing them means losing them.
entries.fix: Rule-based payment fraud checks, and a chargeback case with evidence and deadlines.
entries.blockedNote: Ready. 5.7.92 restated chargebacks; still no dispute model.
entries.closedBy: Chargeback and FraudRule. **A chargeback is not a refund** — a bank decides, on a clock the venue does not control, and a deadline missed is a case lost regardless of merit. Sorted by evidenceDueBy rather than date received. **Accepting is a legitimate outcome and is recorded as a decision**, because a 40 AED case with a 30 AED fee is one to concede deliberately rather than by forgetting. FraudRule **holds rather than refuses** — declining outright turns a false positive into a lost sale.

entries.what: Payment-terminal behaviour is unstated — EMV certification, offline floor limits, payment-server topology.
entries.why: `paymentTerminal` is a device kind with a driver under ADR-0015, which is the right shape. **What is missing is the risk position**: a floor limit below which a terminal authorises offline is a decision about how much fraud a venue will absorb during a network outage, and ADR-0013 makes offline the normal case rather than the exception here.
entries.fix: State the offline authorisation limit and the terminal integration mode.
entries.closedBy: PaymentProvider.terminal — EMV certification, offline floor limit, signature and tip-on-terminal. **A floor limit of zero means a till stops when the line does**, which is the trade-off a venue should make knowingly.

entries.what: The wallet holds one balance and one bonus balance, with one expiry.
entries.why: 4.3.5 asks for distinct credit types — cash, bonus, redemption — **each with its own expiry**, and 4.3.19 asks for first-expiry-first-out consumption across them. `Wallet.expiresAt` is a single date for the whole balance, so **FEFO has nothing to order and bonus credit expiring before cash credit cannot be expressed**. This is also an accounting question: cash credit is a refundable liability and promotional credit usually is not, and `finance` recognises breakage against both identically today. Spending limits and parent-to-child allocation sit on the same model.
entries.fix: Model wallet credit as typed buckets with individual expiry, and consume by first expiry.
entries.blockedNote: Ready. 5.x walked without typed wallet credits appearing.
entries.closedBy: Wallet.credits — cash, bonus, redemption, refund and goodwill, each with its own expiry, consumed first-expiry-first-out. **The expiries are the reason this is a list**: cash a guest paid for should outlive a promotional credit they were given, and a single expiresAt either expires the money they paid or never expires the promotion. **isRefundable is true only for cash** — a wallet that lets a guest cash out a promotion has given it away twice.

entries.what: Peer-to-peer wallet transfer is declared and unreachable.
entries.why: **`WalletTransactionKind` includes `transfer` and no operation performs one.** The enum value exists, the ledger would record it, and there is no path to create it — the CF-49 shape inside a single contract. `games.transferGameCard` is the precedent one contract over, including its rule that balances move whole rather than splitting.
entries.fix: A guest-callable wallet transfer, following the transferGameCard precedent.
entries.closedBy: transferWalletBalance. **Only cash credit transfers** — a promotion that can be moved between guests is a promotion that can be sold, and **a venue that gave 50 dirhams of bonus credit has just funded a secondary market.** Cross-tenant transfer is a payment and belongs on the payment path.

entries.what: No batch or lot instance carrying its own expiry date, and no expiry alerting.
entries.why: **Corrected after reading the schema rather than searching for words.** `isPerishable` and `shelfLifeDays` are on the item, so a shelf life is declared per product. What is absent is the *instance* — a batch or lot on a stock movement with its own expiry — which is what a recall traces and what an expiry alert fires on. `fnb.recordWaste` accepts reason `expired` and nothing knows when a specific delivery expires.
entries.fix: Batch and lot on stock movements, with expiry and alerting.
entries.blockedNote: **Settled by the client at the 18 August F&B, Retail, Procurement & Inventory workshop.** **Decision: *expiry tracking must be maintained at batch/date level*** — the exact granularity this entry identified as missing. Reorder and alert configuration confirmed alongside it, which is CF-134.
entries.closedBy: StockBatch with its own expiry and lot number, plus listExpiringBatches. **isPerishable and shelfLifeDays were on the item, so a shelf life was declared and never instantiated** — two deliveries of the same milk a week apart were one stock level with one implied expiry, and the older was invisible. **A recall names a lot number**, and an inventory that cannot resolve one has to discard everything. Ordered by expiry rather than value, because **the cheapest thing expiring today matters more than the most expensive thing expiring next month.**

entries.what: No supplier invoice management and no three-way match.
entries.why: Purchase orders and goods receipts both exist, so two legs of the match are there. **The third — the supplier invoice — is absent, and the match of order to receipt to invoice is where procurement fraud and overbilling are caught.** It also connects to `finance`, since an approved invoice is a payable.
entries.fix: Supplier invoices with a three-way match against order and receipt.
entries.blockedNote: Ready. 15.3.15 restated three-way matching; the supplier invoice remains the missing third leg.
entries.closedBy: PurchaseOrder.supplierInvoiceRef and matchStatus. **Two legs existed and the third did not — a three-way match with two legs is a two-way match**, and it is the supplier invoice that carries the price nobody has checked. **Price and quantity variance are separated because they have different owners.**

entries.what: No costing method behind stock valuation.
entries.why: **Withdrawn 18 August — the verdict behind it was wrong.** `CostingMethod` exists on `CreateInventoryItemRequest` as `weightedAverage`, `fifo`, `standardCost` and `lastPurchasePrice`, set per item. The original search looked for the method names as free text and missed the enum, which is the same false-negative class the escaped-pipe warning in `find-capability.py` was added to catch. **LIFO is absent and that is correct** — it is prohibited under IFRS, which 5.7.22 requires.
entries.closedBy: Withdrawn. 4.5.35 reverdicted CONTRACTED against createInventoryItem.

entries.what: No server assignment, and no transfer of a check between operators.
entries.why: `setTableLayout` places tables and `openTableVisit` opens one against a principal. **Nothing assigns a server to a section or moves a visit to another server**, which is how a restaurant is organised at shift change and how sales and tips are attributed. `workforce.RotaAssignment` carries position and workstation, so the staffing half exists one contract over.
entries.fix: Assign a server to tables, and reassign an open visit.
entries.blockedNote: **Settled by the client at the 18 August F&B, Retail, Procurement & Inventory workshop.** **Confirmed indirectly: the per-table activity log includes a *Change Server* action**, which requires the server assignment this entry identified as absent.
entries.closedBy: transferTableVisit. **A shift change mid-service leaves a check with a server who has gone home**, and the transfer is recorded rather than silent because tips and sales attribution follow the server — **a check that changes hands without a record is a dispute at cash-up.**

entries.what: Theoretical recipe cost is never compared with actual consumption.
entries.why: `Recipe` carries yield, ingredients and `costPerPortion`; `recordWaste` captures loss with a reason; `inventory` holds every movement. **All three inputs exist and nothing computes the variance**, which is the single most useful number in F&B cost control and the one that finds portioning drift and theft.
entries.fix: A theoretical-versus-actual variance over a period.
entries.blockedNote: **Settled by the client at the 18 August F&B, Retail, Procurement & Inventory workshop.** **Confirmed: production execution and batch management tracks planned versus actual versus yield with batch losses, and wastage must be recorded per item to keep costing accurate** — which is the theoretical-versus-actual variance this entry asked for, stated as a client requirement.
entries.closedBy: ProductionRun.actualQuantity against the recipe theoretical. **The gap is waste, theft, or a recipe that is wrong** — and a kitchen that never compares them cannot tell which.

entries.what: No allergen register, no nutritional values, and no approved substitution path.
entries.why: **`fnb-menuPublished` carries `allergensChanged`, so allergens are modelled enough to notify on change and not enough to state what they are.** 4.6.37 is the sharp one: substituting an ingredient changes the allergen set, and doing that without updating what the guest is told is a safety failure rather than a data one. Recipe versioning (BL-058) matters here too — after an incident the question is what the recipe contained on the day.
entries.fix: An allergen and nutrition register on the recipe, and a substitution path that updates both.
entries.closedBy: Allergen and Nutrition on the menu item. **Fourteen declarable allergens is a legal list, not a preference**, and contains versus mayContain are different claims: one is a recipe fact, the other is a kitchen fact about shared equipment. **A fryer shared with breaded fish makes chips a fish risk and nothing in the recipe says so.**

entries.what: No buzzer or pager association with an order.
entries.why: `FnbOrderStatus.ready` is a state and `tenancy.DeviceKind` has no pager. A buzzer number recorded against an order is a small field with a real operational purpose — it is how a counter outlet hands off without a queue — and `KitchenTicket` already carries `tableLabel` as the same kind of physical reference.
entries.fix: A collection reference on the order, following the tableLabel precedent.
entries.closedBy: KitchenTicket.buzzerCode. Recorded against the order, so **a lost buzzer is a lookup rather than an argument.**

entries.what: No production planning, batch runs, production sheets or central kitchen.
entries.why: **Nothing anywhere** for production plan, batch production, commissary or central kitchen. A commissary supplying several outlets is a producing location transferring to consuming ones, which `inventory.createStockTransfer` could carry — but production consumes ingredients to create a different item, and no movement type expresses that transformation.
entries.fix: A production run consuming ingredients and yielding an item, and a transfer relationship for a commissary.
entries.blockedNote: **Settled by the client at the 18 August F&B, Retail, Procurement & Inventory workshop.** **Confirmed: production execution and batch management, and requisitions from an outlet to the central warehouse.** The commissary relationship is named.
entries.closedBy: ProductionRun with a producing outlet and forOutletIds. **Orders consumed stock and nothing produced any**, so a central kitchen making 400 portions at 6am for four outlets had no representation. **Production is a stock movement in both directions at once** — treating it as two unrelated adjustments loses the yield.

entries.what: Restaurant waitlist, overbooking controls and no-show policy are thin.
entries.why: `TableReservationStatus` includes `noShow`, so the outcome is recorded and **nothing acts on it** — no deposit, no cancellation penalty, no blacklist. Combined tables and occupancy rules preventing overbooking are not modelled, and a restaurant waitlist is not distinguished from a ride queue, though the mechanics differ: a ride queue calls you to a fixed place, a table waitlist calls you when a resource frees.
entries.fix: Waitlist, overbooking rules and a no-show policy on reservations.
entries.blockedNote: **Settled by the client at the 18 August F&B, Retail, Procurement & Inventory workshop.** **Decision on the status flow: Available → Ordered → Table Closed (post payment) → Reserved, with a separate *Cleaning* status explicitly rejected.** `TableReservationStatus` is booked, confirmed, seated, completed, cancelled, noShow — **it does not match the agreed flow** and needs reconciling. An optional deposit adjusted against the bill is also confirmed, which is BL-139.
entries.closedBy: RestaurantWaitlist. **Distinct from queue, which is for rides** — party size, seating preference, walk-away point.  exists so **a guest who leaves is not counted as a guest who was served** in the wait-time report a manager reads. holdExpiresAt is a setting because too short loses a guest returning from the bathroom and too long leaves the table empty at peak.

entries.what: No coursing — fire-and-forget, hold-and-fire, phased, timed or delayed ordering.
entries.why: **Nothing anywhere.** A kitchen ticket is created and sent; there is no held line released later, and no course sequence. This is how fine dining is served — starters fire, mains hold until the table is cleared — and `KitchenTicket.targetReadyAt` is exactly the field a course time would use.
entries.fix: A course and a hold state on kitchen ticket lines.
entries.blockedNote: **Settled by the client at the 18 August F&B, Retail, Procurement & Inventory workshop.** **Decision, with the timer semantics specified:** course-wise ordering groups orders by course so the kitchen fires each at the right time, and **a live *fired* timer on each kitchen ticket tracks elapsed time since the order was sent — not a countdown — and resets when a course within that ticket completes.** `KitchenTicket.elapsedSeconds` is the right field and the reset-per-course rule is new.
entries.closedBy: KitchenTicket.coursing. **Starters before mains is the entire job of a kitchen pass** and the model fired everything at once. Without it a table gets dessert while eating its starter.

entries.what: A guest locked out has no recovery path.
entries.why: `requestGuestOtp` and `verifyGuestOtp` authenticate, and `revokeAllSessions` and `listActiveSessions` manage sessions. **Password reset, username recovery and account unlock are not operations** — the guest-facing half of account management stops at login. `forceLogout` exists for staff and has no guest equivalent for recovery.
entries.fix: Guest password reset, recovery and unlock, following the OTP path already built.
entries.closedBy: PasswordPolicy.recoveryMethods, ordered by strength. **Lockout existed and recovery did not**, which turns a forgotten password into a support call.

entries.what: No store for guest photos, avatars, IDs or signed documents.
entries.why: `assets` is the tenant media library — banners, product images, work-order evidence. **A guest ID scan, a signed waiver or a profile photo is personal data with a different retention posture, a different residency question under ADR-0009, and an erasure obligation** that `cross-cell.createDsarRequest` would have to reach. Putting them in the tenant library would make a DSAR delete a banner or miss a passport.
entries.fix: A guest document store with retention and erasure, separate from the tenant media library.
entries.closedBy: GuestDocument, deliberately separate from assets. **A guest passport scan is not a marketing asset** — different retention clock, different access rule, and one careless query against a shared store returns both. retainUntil is required.

entries.what: Dietary, accessibility and internal-note fields have no structured home, and a guest-level blacklist does not exist.
entries.why: `GuestProfile.tags` is a free list and carries VIP-style markers adequately. **Dietary restrictions and accessibility requirements are health-adjacent personal data** and deserve their own consent and retention treatment rather than a tag. Separately, `access.BlacklistEntry` blacklists a **media code** — a guest barred from the venue can buy a new ticket and get a new code, so a guest-level bar does not exist.
entries.fix: Structured preference fields, and a subject-level bar distinct from the media blacklist.
entries.closedBy: Structured dietary and accessibility fields on the guest profile rather than tags — **health-adjacent personal data deserves its own consent and retention**. Plus GuestIdentification.isBarred, a subject-level bar: the media blacklist blocks a code, and a barred guest presenting a different wristband walks in.

entries.what: Lockers are not modelled, and parking is an entitlement of a different shape.
entries.why: 5.5.8b lists what a portfolio holds: tickets, memberships, passes, experiences, **lockers**, parking and meal plans. `orders` entitlement kinds include `locker` and **nothing anywhere issues, assigns or releases one** — the enum value exists and is unreachable, the CF-49 shape again. Parking has its own `ParkingEntitlement` rather than being an entitlement kind, which is defensible and means a portfolio view has to assemble two models. **Unblocked 18 August** — held on CF-125, now closed. **A blocker that outlives its conflict is the backlog decaying in the way this apparatus exists to prevent**, and this is the second time in one day it happened.
entries.fix: Decide whether lockers are a resource (CF-125) or an entitlement kind, and unify the portfolio view.
entries.blockedNote: Ready. 7.4.16 restated it — locker tickets, against a `locker` entitlement kind nothing issues.
entries.closedBy: Resource.kind gains . ** was an entitlement kind in orders and nothing issued, assigned or released one** — a locker is a specific object checked out to a named guest and returned, which is the resources context exactly. ** is listed to be refused**: it is a balance rather than an object and resolves to retail.Wallet with a mealPlan credit kind.

entries.what: A queue has one capacity, no type and no operating window.
entries.why: `CreateQueueRequest` carries capacityPerCycle, cycleMinutes, maxPartySize, returnWindowMinutes, heightRequirementCm and fastPassAllocationPercent — a well-judged set for one lane. 5.6 asks for **nine queue types**, capacity varying by hour, day, ticket type, membership or channel, and operating hours with booking cut-offs. Today each variation is a separate queue record, which multiplies configuration and splits the wait-time estimate.
entries.fix: Queue kind, a capacity calendar and an operating window.
entries.closedBy: Queue.kind with seven types, operatingWindows and parentQueueId. **A ride has several queues and the model had one** — a single-rider line and a standby line draw from one capacity and fill at different rates, so modelling them as one makes both wait estimates wrong. **accessible is not a courtesy lane**: it has its own capacity because a guest who cannot stand in a switchback needs a place to wait, not priority. lastEntryMinutesBefore exists because **a guest joining two minutes before close waits twenty and is turned away at the front.**

entries.what: No load balancing, no automatic queue assignment and no in-queue offers.
entries.why: Redirecting a guest to a less busy ride, assigning them automatically by ticket type and capacity, and offering an F&B upsell while they wait are three uses of one missing thing: **the queue knows a guest's position and nothing acts on it**. `getWaitTimes` already ranks every queue with provenance, so the input for balancing exists.
entries.fix: Recommendation over the existing wait-time data, and a queue-context placement for upsell rules.
entries.closedBy: Queue.loadBalanceWithQueueIds and inQueueOfferEnabled. **Load balancing is an offer, not an assignment** — a guest sent to a ride they did not choose is a guest who feels managed. **A guest with twenty minutes to wait is a guest with twenty minutes to buy something**, which is the only reason a virtual queue earns its infrastructure.

entries.what: No custom account types, and no notes, annotations or tags on an account.
entries.why: `AccountType` is a closed enum of asset, liability, equity, revenue and expense — **which is correct accounting** and does not meet 5.7.27 as written. Worth pushing back on rather than building: a sixth account type is not a thing in double-entry, and what the client probably wants is sub-classification, which `parentId` and tagging would give.
entries.fix: Confirm whether custom types means sub-classification, then add tags and notes rather than types.
entries.closedBy: Account.subType, tags and notes. **AccountType stays a closed enum because that is correct accounting** — a venue wanting *Deferred Revenue — Annual Pass* is asking for a sub-type, not a sixth type.

entries.what: No deposit liability, and a reservation cannot take payment.
entries.why: `deferredRevenue` covers a sold entitlement not yet consumed. **A deposit is different** — money taken before the sale is complete, held as a liability, released on fulfilment or refunded on cancellation — and `createReservation` takes no payment at all today, so the operational half is missing as well as the accounting one. This is what BL-072's payment link would collect, and what a table-reservation no-show penalty would forfeit.
entries.fix: A deposit on a reservation, posting to a liability account and releasing on fulfilment.
entries.blockedNote: **Settled by the client at the 18 August F&B, Retail, Procurement & Inventory workshop.** **Confirmed: the reservation module includes an optional deposit adjusted against the final bill.** The liability model this entry describes now has a named use case.
entries.closedBy: Deposit and settleDeposit. **A deposit is not deferred revenue and the distinction is a balance-sheet one** — deferred revenue is a sold entitlement not yet consumed, and a deposit is money held against a sale that has not happened. Three outcomes and **none of them is a refund**.

entries.what: No invoice, no credit memo, and no statement of what a compliant receipt must show.
entries.why: `subscription.generateInvoice` bills tenants for the platform. **A tax invoice in the UAE has a mandated format** — supplier TRN, sequential number, prescribed fields, Arabic where required — and issuing one that does not comply is a VAT matter rather than a document-formatting one. `LegalEntity.taxRegistrationNumber` exists, so the data is there and the document is not. Credit memos are the paired obligation: a refund against a tax invoice needs one. **5.10.3 is the same gap at the till** — nothing states which fields a VAT receipt must carry.

entries.what: Nine recognition and journal behaviours the schedule model does not reach.
entries.why: `RecognitionSchedule` and `runRecognition` are strong on the main path. What is unreached: **two schedules may both claim a product kind and nothing resolves which wins**, which is a silent double-recognition; changing an entitlement's validity does not re-time its deferred balance; credit write-off is not a posting event type; recognition is raised at sale site rather than admission site; frequency is driven by the fiscal period rather than configurable; a named account-to-account transfer has no operation or validation; and available balance and account-combination checks do not exist beyond `isPostable`.
entries.fix: Resolve rule precedence first — it is the one that loses money silently.
entries.closedBy: RecognitionSchedule.priority, recognitionSite, frequency and revalidateOnValidityChange, plus recordWriteOff and validateRecognitionSchedules. **Two schedules could both claim a product kind and nothing resolved which won** — a silent double-recognition, and the worst kind of accounting defect because the numbers look plausible. **Equal priority on the same kind is refused at save rather than resolved at run time.** recognitionSite exists because a ticket sold at one venue and admitted at another earns at the gate. **A write-off is not a refund and not a discount** — one returns money that was taken, the other recognises money that will never arrive.

entries.what: No suspense account.
entries.why: **Nothing anywhere** for suspense, unmapped revenue or reclassification. Today a posting event with no account mapping has no destination — and a suspense account is exactly the control that turns a mapping gap into a visible balance somebody clears, rather than a silent imbalance found at close. It also resolves 5.12.103, which asks for one-sided manual entries and **contradicts 5.12.107 and 5.12.108 in the same section**: a one-sided entry is only coherent when the other side is suspense.
entries.fix: A suspense account per legal entity, automatic routing of unmapped postings, and a reclassification operation.
entries.closedBy: Account.isSuspense. **A suspense balance is a work queue, not a resting place** — it should trend to zero, and a balance that grows is the signal a mapping is missing. Which is why it exists rather than the posting being refused.

entries.what: `DataSource` names fourteen sources and several reporting requirements need data outside them.
entries.why: `DataSource` is orders, orderLines, payments, refunds, shifts, scanEvents, entitlements, products, inventory, stockMovements, guests, campaigns, cases and ledgerEntries — **a well-chosen set that stops short of six things the matrix asks reports about**: stock counts and variance (6.1.21), workstations, devices and principals (6.1.28), loyalty positions (6.1.37), reviews and ratings (6.1.46), queue entries and ride throughput (6.1.55), and waste. **This is the BL-053 pattern from the other side** — a generic builder makes every reporting requirement look covered, and the enum is where coverage actually stops. Each addition is a source declaration rather than new data, since every one of these already persists.
entries.fix: Extend DataSource with stockCounts, workstations, principals, loyalty, reviews, queueEntries and waste, each with its field set and personal-data marking.
entries.closedBy: DataSource extended from 15 to 23 — stockCounts, waste, workstations, devices, principals, loyalty, reviews, queueEntries. **Each because the matrix asks for a report the builder could not source**: 6.1.28 wanting who did what at which till is the question an auditor asks first. REPORT_EXPORT_PII gates the four that name a person.

entries.what: No password policy, no account lockout, no forced change at first logon, and principal status is only active or not.
entries.why: **`identity` handles federated authentication well** — OIDC and SAML2 SSO with group mappings, MFA across TOTP, SMS, email, biometric and hardware token, guest OTP, session listing and revocation. **Local password management is absent entirely**: nothing anywhere for password policy, lockout or failed-login handling, and 7.1.8 requires a forced change at first logon which has no path. A venue whose staff do not use SSO — which is the normal case for a seasonal till operator — has no credential lifecycle at all. Principal status also collapses suspended, locked, disabled and pending-approval into `isActive`.
entries.fix: Password policy, failed-login lockout, forced first-logon change, and a principal status enum.
entries.closedBy: PasswordPolicy. **Modelled on NIST SP 800-63B rather than on habit** — length beats composition, and requireBreachCheck stops more account takeovers than every composition rule combined. **maxAgeDays defaults to null on purpose**: forced rotation produces Summer2026! becoming Summer2027!, and it exists because some tenants are contractually obliged to have it rather than because it works. **Lockout is temporary** — permanent lockout on failed attempts is a denial-of-service anybody can run against a known username.

entries.what: Configurable concurrent logins contradicts ADR-0004.
entries.why: **ADR-0004 is single session per user, deliberately.** 7.1.10 asks for the number of concurrent logins to multiple terminals to be configurable. These cannot both be true, and the ADR's reasoning should be tested against the operational case the client has in mind — a supervisor moving between three tills during a rush is the likely one, and `selectRole` plus fast re-login may already answer it. **Unblocked 18 August** — held on CF-130, now closed.
entries.fix: Put the operational case to the client, then either confirm ADR-0004 or amend it.
entries.closedBy: PasswordPolicy.maxConcurrentSessions, null. **ADR-0004 makes a session a token with no server-side registry**, so counting concurrent sessions means adding one — a stateful check on a deliberately stateless design. **Configurable to null is still an answer**, and the contradiction is recorded rather than resolved by quietly building a session table.

entries.what: No device, browser, IP or location restriction on access.
entries.why: **Nothing anywhere.** `Session` records the workstation it opened on and nothing constrains where a login may originate. This is ordinarily a baseline control for a back office holding financial and guest data, and it is also the enforcement half of several 3.3 and 7.1 contextual-access requirements that CF-130 otherwise covers. **Unblocked 18 August** — held on CF-130, now closed.
entries.fix: Restrict sessions by registered device, network and country.
entries.closedBy: PasswordPolicy.deviceRestriction — IP ranges, countries, registered device. **Staff principals, not guests**: a guest restricted to one device cannot use their new phone. **Warn before block by default**, because an IP restriction that blocks silently is a venue manager locked out when their ISP rotates an address.

entries.what: No segregation-of-duties enforcement, no privileged-user governance, no permission review, and no permission delegation.
entries.why: **The package enforces SoD in exactly one place** — the product lifecycle guard requiring the approver not be the author — and there is no general rule stopping a principal holding both create and approve on refunds, promotions or wallet adjustments. 7.1.23 names that combination directly. **`approvals.createApprovalDelegation` exists**, so delegating an *approval* is modelled; delegating a *permission* is not. And grants carry `validFrom` and `validTo`, so they expire — nobody is ever asked to re-confirm the ones that do not, which is what 7.1.33's periodic review exists for. **These are audit findings rather than features** for an operator of this size.
entries.fix: Conflicting-permission rules, a privileged-permission marking, and a periodic access review.
entries.closedBy: SegregationRule. **The package enforced SoD in exactly one place** — the product approver-not-author guard — and there was no general rule. **Checked at grant time, not use time**: discovering a conflict when somebody exercises it means it already existed. **allowWithCompensatingControl exists because a small venue cannot always separate duties**, and a rule that cannot be satisfied gets disabled entirely.

entries.what: No enforced naming schema, no mandatory channel or segment tagging, no code auto-generation, and segments are flat.
entries.why: `Product.code` and `channels` exist and nothing requires a format or a value. 7.3.4 specifies `[ParkCode]-[ProductType]-[Variant]` and 7.3.5 makes a channel and segment tag mandatory — **both are validation rules, and a catalogue of thousands of products drifts within weeks without them.** 7.4.5 separately asks for three-level customer segments where `createSegment` is flat.
entries.fix: Product code validation with generation, required tagging, and a segment hierarchy.
entries.closedBy: Product.segmentTags, hierarchical rather than flat, and codeSchema for the 7.3.4 pattern. **Validation is the point, not the string** — a code typed by hand is a code that will not sort.

entries.what: No subject-access export of one guest's data.
entries.why: **DSAR is well built** — `createDsarRequest` with `pii.erase_subject` propagating and `ai.removeIndexEntry` as the vector-store path — and it covers erasure. **The access half is thinner**: 7.3.10 asks for a guest's data exported in PDF, Excel, CSV or JSON, which `reporting.exportReportResult` does not serve because a report is a population and a subject access request is one person across every contract.
entries.fix: A subject-access export assembling one guest across contracts.
entries.closedBy: exportSubjectData. **A subject access request has a statutory clock**, and answering it by hand across twenty-seven contracts is how a venue misses it. **Assembled from the lineage rather than a hand-written list** — a hand-maintained list of personal data drifts the first time somebody adds a column. **Excludes another guest data even where the two share a booking**, which is what makes this harder than a table dump.

entries.what: No invitation model — campaigns, responses, quotas, lifecycle or per-invitee tokens.
entries.why: **`ApprovalKind.complimentaryTicket` exists, so approving a comp is modelled and issuing an invitation is not.** 7.5 asks for invitation campaigns to VIPs, sponsors and corporate guests, with accept, decline and tentative responses, reminders, quotas allocated to a sponsor and tracked as issued, redeemed and remaining, and a unique token per invitee preventing duplicate registration. **8.1.3–8.1.5 under CF-74 ask for the same capability from the accounting side** — managing invitation PLUs, recording who offered one, and restricting issuance by user profile — so it appears twice in the matrix under two owners. **Unblocked 18 August** — held on CF-74, now closed. **A blocker that outlives its conflict is the backlog decaying in the way this apparatus exists to prevent**, and this is the second time in one day it happened.
entries.fix: An invitation with a quota, a response and a token, resolving CF-74's issuance half at the same time.
entries.closedBy: InvitationCampaign and Invitation. **A campaign broadcasts; an invitation is addressed and expects a response.** quota is places and overInvitePercent is invitations — **a press night invites 150 for 100 seats because 60% come.** The token is single-use, because a link forwarded to a group chat is the failure mode.

entries.what: No AI-generated dashboards, no provider failover, and no embedded analytics.
entries.why: `generateConfiguration` produces a payload against a named target operation and **a dashboard is not among its kinds**, though `createDashboard` is exactly the shape it generates for everything else. Separately, `AiProvider.priority` implies an ordering and **nothing acts on it** — `failureReason` includes `unreachable` and `modelUnavailable` and no failover is stated, which matters because ADR-0009 scopes providers by region and a regional outage takes the assistant down.
entries.fix: Add dashboard as a generation kind, and state failover behaviour on the provider list.
entries.closedBy: AiProvider.failoverProviderId and degradeGracefully. **A provider outage with no fallback is every AI surface going dark at once.** Failover is declared per capability because a provider is — **a fallback covering chat and not embedding leaves search broken while the concierge works.** And where nothing answers, the surface degrades: **an AI feature that returns a 500 is worse than one that quietly becomes ordinary software.**

entries.what: Nothing evaluates a threshold or raises an operational alert, anywhere in the package.
entries.why: **Five sections ask for it and this is the same gap as the event-trigger one at BL-052, seen from the operational side.** 6.1.57 wants exception reports when a KPI leaves range; 8.7.22 wants KPI alerts; 8.2.20 and 8.2.41 want forecast and capacity alerts; 8.9.3 wants queue alerts; 2.1.15 wants an alert when a device stops. **The conditions are all detected already** — `RegisteredDevice.status` reaches `error`, `ShiftCloseResult.requiresAcceptance` fires on variance, `QueueFeedHealth.isHealthy` goes false, `WaitTime.isStale` marks a dead sensor. Every one is computed and none of them tells anybody. **An operations command centre whose alerts a person has to notice on a screen is a screen, not a command centre**, and the decision is whether alerting is a platform capability or a per-contract one. **Unblocked 18 August** — held on CF-134, now closed. **A blocker that outlives its conflict is the backlog decaying in the way this apparatus exists to prevent**, and this is the second time in one day it happened. **Lane changed to deferred 18 August** — the decision behind it was taken (CF-134, CF-131, CF-125) and what remains is build, not a conversation.
entries.closedBy: AlertRule and Alert. **Six contracts detect their own trouble and none told a person** — this is BL-052 seen from the operational side: that one tells a guest something happened, this tells an operator something is wrong. **The window stops it firing on noise** and the cooldown stops it becoming something people close. Acknowledged rather than dismissed, because that records who saw it, and resolution is automatic when the metric returns to range — **an alert only a person can close is a list that only grows.**

entries.what: A game reader has no display behaviour, no per-game entitlement, no retry pricing and no re-tap delay.
entries.why: `games` is well built on the money — `GameCard` with credits, bonus and points, `recordGamePlay` offline-capable and deducting credits while awarding points in one operation, and load creating a liability rather than revenue. **What is missing sits at the reader.** 10.2.14 and 10.2.17 want a different colour for a free game and both normal and VIP price on one unit — **the price shown depends on who tapped**, so the entitlement has to be evaluated at the reader and returned as presentation. 10.2.8 and 10.2.11 want a ticket entitling specific games and the entitlement does not reference one. **10.2.18's re-tap delay is the sharp one**: it stops a single tap being read twice, and `recordGamePlay` carries a sequence for offline replay with nothing debouncing at the device — a double charge on a child's card is the complaint that follows.
entries.fix: Evaluate entitlement at the reader and return display state; add retry pricing and a debounce interval.
entries.closedBy: ReaderProfile. **A guest at an arcade machine cannot read a message, they can only see a light** — display behaviour per outcome, because the interaction is a second long across a noisy room. **A retry after a machine fault is not a second play**, and without it a guest whose game crashed pays twice and the attendant refunds by hand.

entries.what: Out-of-office rerouting, email-link approval, reopening a decided approval, and a shared approval centre.
entries.why: `approvals` answers 80 requirements at a high rate — matrices with amount, risk and condition rules, four modes, levels, SLA, escalation, MFA and signature, delegation, draft, withdrawal and expiry. **Four things it does not reach.** `evaluateApprovalRequirement` returns `noApproverAvailable` and nothing acts on it, which is out-of-office rerouting. Email-link approval is a different authentication path from a session and needs its own token model. Reopening a completed approval is arguably a control the client should not want, and is worth confirming rather than building. A shared service centre spanning tenants is not expressible under cell isolation — ADR-0001.
entries.fix: Reroute on noApproverAvailable; confirm the other three with the client.
entries.closedBy: ApprovalRequest rerouteOnNoApprover, outOfOfficeDelegateId, allowEmailApproval and reopenedFrom. **An approver on leave is an approval that waits for them to come back**, and workforce already knows who is on leave. **Email approval is the weakest path in the system**, so it is off by default. **Reopening creates a new approval that points back** — editing a decision in place destroys what was originally approved.

entries.what: No outbound webhooks and no third-party workflow integration.
entries.why: Domain events are defined per contract and consumed inside the platform. **Nothing publishes to an external subscriber.** 11.1.66 and 12.1.53 both ask for webhooks and 11.1.65 asks for integration with a third-party workflow system. This is a platform capability rather than an approvals one — every contract that emits an event would use it — and it needs delivery guarantees, retry, signing and a subscription model. Belongs with domain 13 Developer & API Management, which has no contract.
entries.fix: An outbound webhook subscription with signing, retry and replay.

entries.what: No developer portal, no developer identity, no rate limiting, no API lifecycle management and no extension marketplace.
entries.why: **Domain 13 has no contract (CF-21) and the walk shows it is not one gap but four separable ones.** **(1) Documentation is closer than it looks** — ADR-0024 makes the contract the deliverable and 25 hand-authored OpenAPI files are the schema documentation; what is missing is a portal rendering them with examples and a try-it console. **(2) A developer is not a partner.** `registerPartner` onboards a commercial reseller with an agreement, credit and commission; a developer building an integration needs an identity, an organisation and credentials, and BL-080 already records the credential half. **(3) Rate limiting has a screen and no operation** — `ADM-015 API Rate Limit & Quota Management` is specified and nothing backs it, which is CF-49's shape. **(4) An extension marketplace is not the module marketplace**: `addLicenceAddOn` enables first-party modules a tenant has bought, where 13.1.50 asks for third-party publishing with certification and presumably revenue share. **The commercial question is whether TICVAI is a platform others build on**, and that is scope, not design.
entries.closedBy: The public-api contract (CF-135). Developer portal, developer identity, rate limiting and API lifecycle. **A partner resells tickets and a developer writes software** — DeveloperAccount.partnerId links them and keeps them separate.

entries.what: No developer sandbox — provisioning, reset, cloning, test data, masking or lifecycle.
entries.why: **The Control Plane already provisions isolated environments** — `provisionCell`, `listEnvironments`, `registerEnvironment`, and ADR-0001 makes a cell the isolation boundary, so data isolation comes free. **A cell is a much heavier unit than a sandbox**, which is the design question: a sandbox that costs a cell will not be handed out freely, and one that shares a cell needs its own isolation story. Masking exists as a concept in `AiPolicy.maskedFields` for prompts and not for a whole environment, and synthetic test data has no generator.
entries.fix: Decide whether a sandbox is a cell, a partition or a mock, then model reset and lifecycle.
entries.closedBy: Sandbox with SyntheticDataProfile and resetSandbox (D2, D3). **Synthetic only, one shared sandbox** — no cloning, no masking, no production data to isolate.

entries.what: No warehouse execution layer — putaway, picking, packing, dispatch or warehouse tasks.
entries.why: **`inventory` models stock as a ledger of movements and that layer is excellent** — two-phase transfers with transit, counts with variance and recount, receipts with rejection. **A warehouse execution layer sits above it and is absent**: a picking list is a work instruction rather than a movement, and putaway rules, packing and dispatch are the operational choreography a WMS adds. `parentLocationId` nests locations so a bin is expressible, and nothing directs anyone to one. **Worth asking whether it is wanted** — a venue with a stockroom needs none of it; one with a central distribution warehouse needs all of it.
entries.fix: Confirm the warehouse operating model before building an execution layer.
entries.blockedNote: **Settled by the client at the 18 August F&B, Retail, Procurement & Inventory workshop.** **Decision: *while the reference material includes many granular statuses — put-away, picking, packing, dispatching — the team agreed NOT to implement every one*.** The entry asked whether a warehouse execution layer was wanted, and the client answered no on the same day. Withdraw the execution layer; keep the ledger.
entries.closedBy: Withdrawn — the client decided against a warehouse execution layer at the 18 August workshop.

entries.what: No request for quotation, no blanket purchase orders and no contract purchasing.
entries.why: `recordQuotation` and `compareQuotations` handle the responses; **nothing issues the request**, so the outbound half of the RFQ cycle is missing and quotes arrive by other means. Blanket orders are the larger gap: a standing agreement drawn against over a period is how a venue buys consumables, each release referencing the blanket rather than being a fresh PO, and it also carries the agreed price that `recordQuotation` would otherwise re-establish every time.
entries.fix: An RFQ issued to suppliers, and a blanket order with releases.
entries.blockedNote: **Settled by the client at the 18 August F&B, Retail, Procurement & Inventory workshop.** **Decision: three purchase order types — Regular, Contract and Service.** Contract PO is *pre-agreed fixed pricing for a defined period, auto-picked*, which is the blanket order this entry asked for, and RFQ is confirmed as *comparing prices from multiple suppliers*. The design question is closed; the build remains.
entries.closedBy: PurchaseOrder.kind with blanket and release, plus rfqId. **A blanket order is a price and a commitment, not a delivery**, and modelling each release as its own order loses the contract that makes the price valid.

entries.what: No firmware deployment, no device-to-asset link, and no device enrolment or retirement lifecycle.
entries.why: **`tenancy` covers more of domain 16 than its name suggests** — twenty device kinds under ADR-0015, heartbeat reporting reachability and consumables, remote configuration through `DeviceBinding`. **Three things it does not reach.** `RegisteredDevice.firmwareVersion` records a version and **nothing deploys one** — a fleet of turnstiles and readers that cannot be updated remotely is a site visit per device, and that is an operating cost rather than a feature. `maintenance` has assets, work orders and plans and **nothing links a device to an asset**, so a venue runs two registers for the same physical object. And `states/registered-device.yaml` states there is no terminal state deliberately — *a device is never finished* — which makes retirement an explicit non-decision worth revisiting now that 16.1.6 asks for it.
entries.closedBy: RegisteredDevice gained batteryPercent, lastCheckedAt and health; Workstation gained healthScore and configurationProfileId (CF-136, closed 20 August). **All nine device kinds the client board names already existed in DeviceKind, which carries twenty** — the list was never the gap. **lastCheckedAt is separate from lastHeartbeatAt because a printer with no paper heartbeats perfectly.**

entries.what: A device does not authenticate to the platform, and there is no tamper detection.
entries.why: **Nothing anywhere** for device authentication, device authorisation, encrypted device communication or tamper detection. `shared/common.yaml` has `serviceAuth` for cell-to-cell and cell-to-Control-Plane, where *there is no user, so the permission model does not apply* — that is a different trust boundary. **A reader on a gate is an unattended endpoint on the venue network**, and ADR-0013's local-first design means it holds an offline package of valid entitlements. A device that cannot prove what it is, on a channel that is not authenticated, holding a bundle of credentials, is the attack surface an access-control system is judged on. This is also CF-69's SIEM question from the device side — `identity.authz_audit` exists and nothing ships security events anywhere. **CF-136 closed 20 August and this half did not.** What an unauthenticated device may do is a security question Qossai has not answered, and it is now held against CF-64 rather than a closed conflict.

entries.what: No downtime measurement, no structured root cause, no work-order escalation, no corrective action as a tracked item, and no spare-parts reservation.
entries.why: **`maintenance` is one of the strongest contracts in the package** — a work-order lifecycle with accept, reject-with-reason, start, pause, resume, complete, verify and close; evidence as *a photo of the fault before and the repair after*; verification separate from completion for safety-critical work; `recordAuthorityNotification` for reportable incidents; inspection templates with retentionYears. **Five things sit just outside it.** `setAssetStatus` takes a ride out of service and **nothing measures how long it was down**, which is the number a maintenance function is judged on and the input to availability. Completion requires a resolution note and no cause taxonomy, so recurring failures cannot be counted. Approval escalation is generic and escalating a *late work order* is a different act. A corrective action from an incident is not distinct from a work order, so it cannot be tracked to a different owner and due date. And **`StockPosition.allocated` exists as a field with nothing reserving against it**, so a planned repair can find its part sold.
entries.fix: Downtime from asset status transitions, a cause taxonomy, time-based work-order escalation, and a parts reservation.
entries.closedBy: WorkOrder.downtimeMinutes, rootCause and escalationLevel. **Downtime is measured out-of-service to back-in-service, not work start to work end** — a ride down six hours of which two were worked is down six hours, and the gap is the thing worth managing. **rootCause is structured because free text cannot be counted**, and deferredMaintenance is the value a venue least wants to see and most needs to. **Escalation is a clock, not a decision.**

entries.what: Staff devices cannot be registered for push, offline scope is unstated for the staff app, and there is no staff-to-staff messaging.
entries.why: **Guest devices register for push — `registerGuestDevice`, `listGuestDevices`, `revokeGuestDevice` with token fingerprint, platform and failure count. Staff devices do not.** `RegisteredDevice` in `tenancy` is a till peripheral with a driver; a technician's phone receiving a work-order push has no registration path at all, and CF-134's alerting has nowhere to deliver on the staff side. Offline is designed carefully where it matters — ADR-0013, `syncScans` with stop-at-sequence, `acknowledgeAnnouncement` queued offline — and **which staff-app operations work offline is not stated as a set**, which is what an engineer needs before building the sync layer. Announcements are one-way; staff-to-staff messaging has no home, since `marketing-crm` conversations are guest-facing. **Unblocked 18 August** — held on CF-134, now closed. **A blocker that outlives its conflict is the backlog decaying in the way this apparatus exists to prevent**, and this is the second time in one day it happened.
entries.fix: Staff device registration mirroring the guest model, a stated offline operation set, and a decision on internal messaging.
entries.closedBy: RegisteredDevice.pushToken, pushPlatform, pushFailureCount and offlineScope. **Guest devices registered for push and staff devices did not** — a scanner that cannot be told anything is a scanner somebody has to walk to. **fullVenue on a personal handset is a decision, not a default**: a device that can do everything offline carries the whole venue data in somebody pocket.

entries.what: No voice interaction — `AiCapability` is chat, embedding, vision and rerank.
entries.why: Speech is not among the capabilities, so neither transcription nor synthesis has a provider slot. **The case the requirement exists for is a technician with gloved hands on a plant room floor**, which is also where a screen is least usable. It carries a residency question under ADR-0009 — audio of a staff member is personal data leaving the region — and a masking question, since `AiPolicy.maskedFields` operates on structured fields and cannot mask speech.
entries.fix: Add a speech capability with its own provider and residency position, or decline it explicitly.
entries.closedBy: AiCapability speechToText and textToSpeech. **Voice added rather than declined, with its own residency position** — speech is the capability where UAE residency is hardest to satisfy, and a guest speaking into a kiosk is producing personal data in the moment.

entries.what: No self-service onboarding, no venue-type templates, no trial state, and licensing has no priced dimension.
entries.why: `subscription` is the Control Plane and handles the **operator-led** path well — createTenant, provisionCell, plans with versions, `previewSubscriptionChange` returning *what would change, what would break, and the prorated amount*, suspend, reactivate, terminate, metering and entitlement usage. **What is absent is the prospect-led path.** There is no trial state to convert from, no venue-type template seeding a working configuration, and 20.3 asks for licensing priced on venue size index, POS count, active users, venues, transaction or attendance volume — **metering exists and the *basis* is not a modelled dimension**, so a hybrid model has nothing to combine. Whether TICVAI is sold self-service at all is a commercial question the phasing paper does not answer.
entries.fix: Confirm whether self-service onboarding is in scope, then model a trial state and a licensing basis.
entries.closedBy: OnboardingApplication and VenueTypeTemplate. **The operator-led path assumes somebody at Softlabs decided this tenant exists** — this is the other one. **Nothing is provisioned until verification passes**, because an unverified application that provisions a cell is a cell somebody has to clean up. **Trial is a state, not a plan**: a prospect trials the plan they will pay for, so conversion is a date change rather than a migration.

entries.what: A seat map holds seats and nothing else — no standing zone, suite, stage, entry, exit or seat view.
entries.why: **`seating` is strong on everything that is a seat** — status, holds with TTL, blocks with reasons and auto-release, buffer and orphan rules, accessible companions, recommendation returning contiguous groups, and a two-phase import validated against real client files. **The map itself is only seats.** `SeatAttribute` has eight values and none is a zone; a standing area is a capacity without individual seats, which is a different primitive. **`layerMapping` on geometry import names a `stageLayer`, so the importer can read a stage and the model cannot hold one** — the same is true of entries and exits, which 21.8.3's accessible route needs to route between. And no seat carries a view image or sightline, so 21.5.18 means a guest cannot see what they are buying.
entries.fix: Non-seat map objects — zones, stage, entries, exits — and a view reference per seat or section.
entries.closedBy: MapZone with twelve kinds. **A standing area is a capacity without individual seats**, and modelling it as seats means inventing numbers nobody prints and a guest cannot find. A suite is the opposite — one sellable unit sold whole. **And a stage or a pillar sells nothing while deciding what the seats behind it are worth**, which is the only reason to draw it.

entries.what: Native CAD and raster image import are not supported formats.
